items.title: Java library for parsing Javadoc comments
items.summary: I would like to be able to programmatically convert Javadoc comments (such as those in the generated code of LWJGL ) to other formats (such as Markdown ). This would allow me to do things like automatically generating an idiomatic Clojure wrapper for LWJGL with human-readable docstrings. I can pick the Javadoc comments out of a source file using JavaParser , but that's where I get stuck.

items.title: Do you know a free program that keeps track of available software updates?
items.summary: I need to keep track of several software applications on my computer in a local network. All my software updates are available within this (offline) network and I am looking for a tool, that keeps track of possible updates. The optimal way would be: The program checks every night for updates within local network and (if the corresponding program is not running), it installs those update. One important addition: I need to keep track of my own programs.

items.title: Firewall app for MacOS that I can quit
items.summary: I know there is a few firewall solutions for Mac, I use one - "Little Snitch" and while it's great, it does not satisfy one of my requirements. My use case is as follows: I'm offline, maybe even in airplane mode, no network connectivity whatsoever and I'm running Mac on battery and just want to maximize its run time. I would like to quit as many apps as possible. Little Snitch would not let me quit/exit the app when/if I do not need it at the time. The only solution to unload it from memory is to uninstall the app.

items.title: How does one build an LLM router with a labelled set of 100 tasks?
items.summary: I already spent the time building rubrics for a set of ~100 tasks on various criterias (accuracy, thoroughness communication style ). How does one go on to build a router based on this ? There appears to be no good literature / open source projects on this. I tried a bunch of approaches with the help of claude: - trying to use Jev via a serious of probe Yes/No questions ( does task contain x, does the world have y ...etc ).

items.title: OpenComputer – an open source alternative to Devin
items.summary: Hi HN! Utpal here, I'm one of the founders of OpenComputer. OpenComputer is an open source cloud coding agent for teams that can run in your own cloud account (AWS, GCP, Azure). We run the agent harness and the sandbox on the same durable VM (architecture in the docs [1]). First commit lands in 24s; the alternatives we benchmarked took 53-72s (benchmarks below [2]). Two other choices: - One VM per team, scalable horizontally. Sessions are isolated in git worktrees. - Session files are backed up to a repo after every turn, so any session can resume on another VM.

deep.body: Hi HN! Utpal here, I'm one of the founders of OpenComputer. OpenComputer is an open source cloud coding agent for teams that can run in your own cloud account (AWS, GCP, Azure). We run the agent harness and the sandbox on the same durable VM (architecture in the docs [1]). First commit lands in 24s; the alternatives we benchmarked took 53-72s (benchmarks below [2]). Two other choices: - One VM per team, scalable horizontally. Sessions are isolated in git worktrees. - Session files are backed up to a repo after every turn, so any session can resume on another VM. We noticed that past ~640 session-hours a month, one always-on 4 vCPU VM is cheaper than per-session E2B sandboxes, for example. So at scale, this setup would not only be faster than current SOTA coding agents, but also more cost-efficient. Feel free to try via cloud for free [4] or self host. We would love any and all feedback, and happy to answer any questions! Full demo below [3]. [1]: https://docs.opencomputer.dev/getting-started/architecture [2]: https://opencomputer.dev/blog/cloud-agents-as-fast-as-local/ [3]: https://x.com/IgorZIJ/status/2121309785882591711 [4]: https://app.opencomputer.dev
